t_acad.t: The Secret Life of Sleep in Animals
x: Almost all animals studied so far show some form of sleep, but the way they sleep varies enormously. Some birds and dolphins can rest one half of their brain at a time, keeping the other half alert. This allows dolphins to keep swimming and surface to breathe, and helps birds watch for predators.

The amount of sleep also differs widely between species. Large plant-eating animals such as giraffes and elephants may sleep only a few hours a day, possibly because they need to spend most of their time eating low-energy food. In contrast, some small animals that eat energy-rich food, such as bats, may sleep for more than eighteen hours.

Despite these differences, scientists believe sleep must have important functions, since it exists across so many species even though sleeping animals are vulnerable to attack. Current theories suggest that sleep helps to save energy, repair the body and process memories.
q: What is the passage mainly about?
How and why sleep differs among animals
Why can dolphins keep swimming while they sleep?
They rest one half of their brain at a time.
Some birds and dolphins can rest one half of their brain at a time, keeping the other half alert.
According to the passage, why might giraffes sleep so little?
They need to spend most of their time eating low-energy food.
possibly because they need to spend most of their time eating low-energy food
The word "vulnerable" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to:
sleeping animals are vulnerable to attack
Why do scientists believe sleep has important functions?
It exists in many species despite being risky.
All animals sleep the same amount.
since it exists across so many species even though sleeping animals are vulnerable to attack

x: Honeybees live in large colonies, and finding enough food for thousands of individuals is a constant challenge. Worker bees called foragers fly out to search for flowers rich in nectar and pollen. When a forager discovers a good source, she returns to the hive and shares the information with her sisters through a remarkable form of communication known as the waggle dance.

The dance is performed on the vertical surface of the honeycomb inside the dark hive. The bee runs forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement. The angle of this straight run compared with the vertical shows the direction of the food relative to the position of the sun. The length of time the bee spends waggling indicates how far away the food is: the longer the waggle, the greater the distance.

This behaviour was first explained in detail by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who received a Nobel Prize in 1973 partly for this work. His experiments showed that bees which watched a dance were able to fly directly to food they had never visited before. Today, researchers still study the waggle dance because it is one of the few known examples of animals communicating about places that are far away and out of sight.
q: What is the passage mainly about?
How honeybees share information about food locations
The life of Karl von Frisch
According to paragraph 2, what does the angle of the straight run show?
The direction of the food relative to the sun
The angle of this straight run compared with the vertical shows the direction of the food relative to the position of the sun.
What does it mean if a bee waggles for a longer time?
The food is closer to the hive.
the longer the waggle, the greater the distance
The word "indicates" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
The length of time the bee spends waggling indicates how far away the food is
The word "His" in paragraph 3 refers to:
His experiments showed that bees which watched a dance were able to fly directly to food they had never visited before.

x: Today I'd like to look at a behaviour we all share but rarely think about: yawning. For a long time, people believed we yawn because our bodies need more oxygen. However, experiments have shown that breathing extra oxygen does not reduce yawning.

A more recent theory suggests that yawning helps to cool the brain. When we yawn, we take in a large amount of air, which may lower the temperature of blood flowing to the head. Supporting this idea, studies have found that people yawn less often when the air around them is very hot.
Finally, yawning is contagious: seeing or even reading about someone yawning can make us yawn. Some researchers think this may be connected to empathy, our ability to share other people's feelings.
q: What is the talk mainly about?
How the brain works during sleep

t_talk.t: Academic talk: why the sky is blue
x: Today we're going to answer a question that children often ask: why is the sky blue? Sunlight looks white, but it is actually a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. Each colour travels as a wave, and blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light.

When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it hits tiny gas molecules in the air. These molecules scatter short wavelengths, like blue, much more strongly than long wavelengths, like red. As a result, blue light is spread across the whole sky, and that is the colour we see when we look up during the day.

This also explains why sunsets are often red and orange. In the evening, sunlight has to travel through much more of the atmosphere to reach our eyes. By the time it arrives, most of the blue light has been scattered away, leaving mainly the reds and oranges.
q: What is the talk mainly about?
Why the sky looks blue and sunsets look red
What does the speaker say about sunlight?

it is actually a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow

Light with long wavelengths, such as red
These molecules scatter short wavelengths, like blue, much more strongly than long wavelengths, like red.
Most blue light has been scattered away before it reaches us.
The sun becomes cooler in the evening.

i_read.t: The Return of the Night Train
x: A. In the 1990s and 2000s, many European night trains were withdrawn as cheap flights became popular and operators struggled to make a profit. Travellers could fly across the continent in a couple of hours, often for less than the price of a train ticket.

B. In recent years, however, night trains have made a comeback. Growing concern about the environmental impact of flying has encouraged many travellers to choose rail, which produces far lower emissions per passenger on most routes. Several new routes have opened, connecting cities such as Vienna, Berlin, Paris and Amsterdam.

C. Supporters point out that night trains also save time and money, as passengers travel while they sleep and do not need to pay for a hotel. Nevertheless, tickets for private sleeping cabins can still be expensive, and demand on popular routes often exceeds the number of available seats.

x: A. For centuries, people have called the dark centre of a pencil its 'lead', but pencils have never actually contained the metal lead. The material inside is graphite, a soft form of carbon. In the sixteenth century, a large deposit of very pure graphite was discovered in Borrowdale, in the north of England. Local people found that it left a clear dark mark, and it was soon being used for writing and drawing.

B. Early users wrapped pieces of graphite in string or sheepskin to keep their hands clean. Later, craftsmen began placing graphite sticks inside wooden holders, creating something close to the modern pencil. However, pure graphite was rare, and when supplies became difficult to obtain, pencil makers needed another solution.

C. In 1795, the French inventor Nicolas-Jacques Conté found that powdered graphite could be mixed with clay and baked in a kiln. By changing the amount of clay, he could make pencils that were harder or softer. This method allowed manufacturers to use lower-quality graphite, and it is still the basis of how most pencils are made today. In many countries, pencils are marked with letters such as H for 'hard' and B for 'black', which describe how firm the core is and how dark a line it produces.
q: Pencils used to contain the metal lead.
pencils have never actually contained the metal lead
The graphite found in Borrowdale was very pure.
a large deposit of very pure graphite was discovered in Borrowdale
Conté sold his pencils mainly to artists.
(The text does not say who bought Conté's pencils.)
Using different amounts of clay changes how hard a pencil is.
By changing the amount of clay, he could make pencils that were harder or softer.
Which heading best fits paragraph B?
From bare graphite to wooden holders
Later, craftsmen began placing graphite sticks inside wooden holders, creating something close to the modern pencil.
What does the letter B on a pencil stand for?

Cacao beans were so valuable that the Aztecs even used them as a form of money.
When cacao reached Europe in the sixteenth century, sugar was added to make the drink sweeter, and it became fashionable among the rich.

x: In this lecture, I'll outline the history of paper, a material we use every day without much thought.
Before paper, people wrote on many different surfaces, including clay tablets, papyrus made from a river plant, and parchment made from animal skin.

Paper as we know it was developed in China. Its invention is traditionally credited to a court official named Cai Lun, around the year one hundred and five. He made sheets from tree bark, old cloth and plant fibres soaked in water.

For several centuries, the technique remained mainly in East Asia. In the eighth century, papermaking reached the city of Samarkand in Central Asia, and soon afterwards Baghdad had its own paper mills.

Paper reached Europe by the twelfth century, but it was still made from old cloth, or rags. Only in the nineteenth century did manufacturers learn to make paper from wood pulp, which made it cheap enough for newspapers and books to be produced in huge numbers.
q: Who is traditionally credited with inventing paper?
A court official named Cai Lun
Its invention is traditionally credited to a court official named Cai Lun

What effect did the use of wood pulp have?
It made paper cheap enough for mass production.
It made paper stronger than parchment.
